Medinan, and its verses number 78 [revealed after al-Ra'd]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Allah, Mighty and Exalted, enumerates His blessings (ala'ahu), and He wished to begin with the first thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, enumerates His blessings, and He wished to mention first the thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: We modify this statement in his words "that the creation of man had as its purpose", i.e., the intended meaning of it: that he should come to know the Books and the revelation, and we substitute that the purpose of creating him is that he be called to that, not that this occurs from him. This is the general meaning. Then among people, some are those whom Allah willed to gain knowledge of the religion, so He facilitated that for them, and among them are those whose misguidance and ignorance He willed, so they moved away from it and were not granted success. And Allah is the Granter of success and the Truth.]] and the varieties of His favours, which is the blessing of religion. So he put first, from the blessing of religion, what is at the highest of its ranks and the furthest of its levels:

This is His bestowal of the Qur'an, its sending down and its teaching, because it is the greatest of Allah's revelations in rank, the highest in station, and the most excellent in its effect in the matters of religion. It is the summit (sinam) of the heavenly Books, their confirmation, and the standard by which they are measured. He delayed the mention of the creation of man after mentioning it, and then followed it with it, so that it would be known that He created him only for the religion, and that he might come to know His revelation and His Books, and that for which man was created. It is as if the purpose in his origination was preceding him and prior to him. Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech (al-bayan), which is the articulate language that expresses what is in the heart [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech, which is the clear, articulate language... etc." Ahmad said: He singled out the first sentences for mention only as a rebuke to man, because of the attachment of their meanings to him. Do you not see that he is mentioned in them explicitly, implicitly, and by omission indicated by the context? So he is spoken of openly in His words ﴿He created man﴾, implicitly in His words ﴿He taught him the bayan﴾, and indicated by omission in His words ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, for it is the second object. As for His words ﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate﴾, there is absolutely no mention of man in them, and most of the purpose of their context is to alert to the greatness of Allah, Exalted.]] ﴿The Most Gracious﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and these verbs together with their pronouns are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifa). Their being free of a conjunction is because they come in the pattern of enumeration, as you say: "Zayd made you rich after poverty, honoured you after humiliation, increased you after scarcity, did to you what no one has done to anyone; so what of His kindness do you deny?"

In this there are great benefits for people, among them knowing the years and calculation. ﴿And the star﴾: and the plant that springs up from the earth without a stem, like herbs. ﴿And the tree﴾: that which has a stem. Their prostration is their submission to Allah in what they were created for, and that they do not refuse, likened to the prostration of the accountable humans in their obedience. If you say: how are these two sentences connected to ﴿the Most Gracious﴾? I say: in them the verbal connection is dispensed with in favour of the connection of meaning, since it is known that the reckoning is His reckoning, and the prostration is to Him and not to other than Him. It is as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him." If you say: how did he omit the conjunction in the first sentences, and then bring it after? I say:

They are rebuked by those first sentences coming in the manner of a threat, so that each sentence stands independently in reproaching those who denied the Most Gracious and His blessings, just as a man who denies the favours of the benefactor is rebuked by enumerating them to him, in the example I mentioned. Then the speech returns to its proper course after the rebuke, in joining what must be joined for the sake of harmony and proximity by means of the conjunction. If you say: what harmony is there between these two sentences, that the conjunction was placed between them? I say: the sun and the moon are heavenly, and the star and the tree are earthly, so between the two categories there is harmony by way of opposition, and the heaven and the earth are never mentioned except as a pair; and the running of the sun and moon by reckoning is of the kind of submission to the command of Allah, so it is fitting with the prostration of the star and the tree. It is said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ means He made it a sign and a sign-post (ayah).

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The man (al-insan) is Adam." And from him also: "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

From Mujahid: "The star (al-najm)": the stars of the sky. ﴿And the heaven He raised﴾: He created it raised and elevated, as He made it the source of His rulings, the origin of His decrees, the place of descent of His commands and prohibitions, and the dwelling of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets. Through this He draws attention to the greatness of His majesty, His dominion and His authority. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. In the reading of Abdullah: ﴿and He lowered the balance﴾. By it He meant everything by which things are weighed and their quantities known, of scale, steelyard, measure and gauge. That is, He created it placed and lowered upon the earth, since He attached to it the rulings of His servants, their decisions, and what He made them responsible for in terms of equity and fairness in their taking and giving. ﴿That you not transgress﴾: lest you transgress; or it is that the "an" is explanatory. Abdullah recited: ﴿la tatghaw﴾ without "an", on the intention of "saying". ﴿And establish the weighing with justice﴾: and make your weighing straight with justice. ﴿And do not skimp in the balance﴾: do not diminish it. This is a command to equity and a prohibition of transgression, which is aggression and excess, and of loss, which is short-measure and deficiency.

The word "balance" is repeated to emphasise the charge concerning it, and to strengthen the command to use it and the urging to it. It has been read: "and the heaven" with a nominative (al-raf'), and "do not skimp" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma and a kasra on the sin, and a fatha as well. It is said: "kharisa al-mizan" (he diminished the balance), "yakhsaruhu" and "yakhsiru." As for the fatha, it is based on the original: "do not skimp in the balance," so the preposition is dropped and the verb is connected. ﴿And the earth He laid out﴾: He spread it out, flattened over the water. ﴿For the creatures (lil-anam)﴾: for the creation, which is everything upon the surface of the earth of living creature. It is said from al-Hasan: "mankind and jinn." So it is like a couch for them, on which they move. ﴿Therein fruit﴾: kinds of what is enjoyed as a delicacy. ﴿And palm-trees (al-akmam)﴾: everything that is enclosed (yukammu), i.e., covered, of fibre, palm-frond and spathe [[His words "wa-sa'fa wa-kafarra" — in the Sihah it says "al-kafara without a ta', and it is the container of the spathe," so perhaps the author's expression is "from its fibre, its frond and its spathe", with "kull" annexed to the pronoun of the palm, as will come in "its fruit, its clusters and its trunks", and the copyist mistook it for the feminine ta' and so cut it off above. (ʿ)]], and all of it is beneficial, just as one benefits from what is enclosed of its fruit, its clusters and its trunks. It is said that al-akmam are the containers of dates; the singular is kimm, with a kasra on the kaf. ﴿And the grain-husk (al-'asf)﴾: the leaves of the crop; it is said it is the chaff. ﴿And the sweet-smelling plant (al-rayhan)﴾: the provision, which is the kernel. He meant in it what is enjoyed of fruits, and what unites enjoyment and nourishment, which is the fruit of the palm, and what is fed upon, which is the grain.

It has been read: "wa-l-rayhani" with a kasra. Its meaning is: "and the grain possessing the husk, which is fodder for livestock, and the sweet plant, which is food for people." With a damma, it is read as "wa-dhu al-rayhan," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun is put in its place.

It is said: its meaning is: "and in it is the sweet-smelling plant which is scented." In the codices of the people of Syria it reads: "and the grain possessing the husk and the sweet plant," meaning: "and He created the grain and the sweet plant," or "and He singled out the grain and the sweet plant." It is permissible that it be meant: "and possessor of the sweet plant," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun put in its place. The address in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ is to the two species (al-thaqalan), by the indication of "the creatures" (al-anam) referring to both of them. And His words ﴿We will surely attend to you, O two species﴾ [are addressed to them].

Allah, Mighty and Exalted, enumerates His blessings (ala'ahu), and He wished to begin with the first thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, enumerates His blessings, and He wished to mention first the thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: We modify this statement in his words "that the creation of man had as its purpose", i.e., the intended meaning of it: that he should come to know the Books and the revelation, and we substitute that the purpose of creating him is that he be called to that, not that this occurs from him. This is the general meaning. Then among people, some are those whom Allah willed to gain knowledge of the religion, so He facilitated that for them, and among them are those whose misguidance and ignorance He willed, so they moved away from it and were not granted success. And Allah is the Granter of success and the Truth.]] and the varieties of His favours, which is the blessing of religion. So he put first, from the blessing of religion, what is at the highest of its ranks and the furthest of its levels:

This is His bestowal of the Qur'an, its sending down and its teaching, because it is the greatest of Allah's revelations in rank, the highest in station, and the most excellent in its effect in the matters of religion. It is the summit (sinam) of the heavenly Books, their confirmation, and the standard by which they are measured. He delayed the mention of the creation of man after mentioning it, and then followed it with it, so that it would be known that He created him only for the religion, and that he might come to know His revelation and His Books, and that for which man was created. It is as if the purpose in his origination was preceding him and prior to him. Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech (al-bayan), which is the articulate language that expresses what is in the heart [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech, which is the clear, articulate language... etc." Ahmad said: He singled out the first sentences for mention only as a rebuke to man, because of the attachment of their meanings to him. Do you not see that he is mentioned in them explicitly, implicitly, and by omission indicated by the context? So he is spoken of openly in His words ﴿He created man﴾, implicitly in His words ﴿He taught him the bayan﴾, and indicated by omission in His words ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, for it is the second object. As for His words ﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate﴾, there is absolutely no mention of man in them, and most of the purpose of their context is to alert to the greatness of Allah, Exalted.]] ﴿The Most Gracious﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and these verbs together with their pronouns are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifa). Their being free of a conjunction is because they come in the pattern of enumeration, as you say: "Zayd made you rich after poverty, honoured you after humiliation, increased you after scarcity, did to you what no one has done to anyone; so what of His kindness do you deny?"

In this there are great benefits for people, among them knowing the years and calculation. ﴿And the star﴾: and the plant that springs up from the earth without a stem, like herbs. ﴿And the tree﴾: that which has a stem. Their prostration is their submission to Allah in what they were created for, and that they do not refuse, likened to the prostration of the accountable humans in their obedience. If you say: how are these two sentences connected to ﴿the Most Gracious﴾? I say: in them the verbal connection is dispensed with in favour of the connection of meaning, since it is known that the reckoning is His reckoning, and the prostration is to Him and not to other than Him. It is as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him." If you say: how did he omit the conjunction in the first sentences, and then bring it after? I say:

They are rebuked by those first sentences coming in the manner of a threat, so that each sentence stands independently in reproaching those who denied the Most Gracious and His blessings, just as a man who denies the favours of the benefactor is rebuked by enumerating them to him, in the example I mentioned. Then the speech returns to its proper course after the rebuke, in joining what must be joined for the sake of harmony and proximity by means of the conjunction. If you say: what harmony is there between these two sentences, that the conjunction was placed between them? I say: the sun and the moon are heavenly, and the star and the tree are earthly, so between the two categories there is harmony by way of opposition, and the heaven and the earth are never mentioned except as a pair; and the running of the sun and moon by reckoning is of the kind of submission to the command of Allah, so it is fitting with the prostration of the star and the tree. It is said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ means He made it a sign and a sign-post (ayah).

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The man (al-insan) is Adam." And from him also: "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

From Mujahid: "The star (al-najm)": the stars of the sky. ﴿And the heaven He raised﴾: He created it raised and elevated, as He made it the source of His rulings, the origin of His decrees, the place of descent of His commands and prohibitions, and the dwelling of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets. Through this He draws attention to the greatness of His majesty, His dominion and His authority. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. In the reading of Abdullah: ﴿and He lowered the balance﴾. By it He meant everything by which things are weighed and their quantities known, of scale, steelyard, measure and gauge. That is, He created it placed and lowered upon the earth, since He attached to it the rulings of His servants, their decisions, and what He made them responsible for in terms of equity and fairness in their taking and giving. ﴿That you not transgress﴾: lest you transgress; or it is that the "an" is explanatory. Abdullah recited: ﴿la tatghaw﴾ without "an", on the intention of "saying". ﴿And establish the weighing with justice﴾: and make your weighing straight with justice. ﴿And do not skimp in the balance﴾: do not diminish it. This is a command to equity and a prohibition of transgression, which is aggression and excess, and of loss, which is short-measure and deficiency.

The word "balance" is repeated to emphasise the charge concerning it, and to strengthen the command to use it and the urging to it. It has been read: "and the heaven" with a nominative (al-raf'), and "do not skimp" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma and a kasra on the sin, and a fatha as well. It is said: "kharisa al-mizan" (he diminished the balance), "yakhsaruhu" and "yakhsiru." As for the fatha, it is based on the original: "do not skimp in the balance," so the preposition is dropped and the verb is connected. ﴿And the earth He laid out﴾: He spread it out, flattened over the water. ﴿For the creatures (lil-anam)﴾: for the creation, which is everything upon the surface of the earth of living creature. It is said from al-Hasan: "mankind and jinn." So it is like a couch for them, on which they move. ﴿Therein fruit﴾: kinds of what is enjoyed as a delicacy. ﴿And palm-trees (al-akmam)﴾: everything that is enclosed (yukammu), i.e., covered, of fibre, palm-frond and spathe [[His words "wa-sa'fa wa-kafarra" — in the Sihah it says "al-kafara without a ta', and it is the container of the spathe," so perhaps the author's expression is "from its fibre, its frond and its spathe", with "kull" annexed to the pronoun of the palm, as will come in "its fruit, its clusters and its trunks", and the copyist mistook it for the feminine ta' and so cut it off above. (ʿ)]], and all of it is beneficial, just as one benefits from what is enclosed of its fruit, its clusters and its trunks. It is said that al-akmam are the containers of dates; the singular is kimm, with a kasra on the kaf. ﴿And the grain-husk (al-'asf)﴾: the leaves of the crop; it is said it is the chaff. ﴿And the sweet-smelling plant (al-rayhan)﴾: the provision, which is the kernel. He meant in it what is enjoyed of fruits, and what unites enjoyment and nourishment, which is the fruit of the palm, and what is fed upon, which is the grain.

It has been read: "wa-l-rayhani" with a kasra. Its meaning is: "and the grain possessing the husk, which is fodder for livestock, and the sweet plant, which is food for people." With a damma, it is read as "wa-dhu al-rayhan," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun is put in its place.

It is said: its meaning is: "and in it is the sweet-smelling plant which is scented." In the codices of the people of Syria it reads: "and the grain possessing the husk and the sweet plant," meaning: "and He created the grain and the sweet plant," or "and He singled out the grain and the sweet plant." It is permissible that it be meant: "and possessor of the sweet plant," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun put in its place. The address in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ is to the two species (al-thaqalan), by the indication of "the creatures" (al-anam) referring to both of them. And His words ﴿We will surely attend to you, O two species﴾ [are addressed to them].

Allah, Mighty and Exalted, enumerates His blessings (ala'ahu), and He wished to begin with the first thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, enumerates His blessings, and He wished to mention first the thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: We modify this statement in his words "that the creation of man had as its purpose", i.e., the intended meaning of it: that he should come to know the Books and the revelation, and we substitute that the purpose of creating him is that he be called to that, not that this occurs from him. This is the general meaning. Then among people, some are those whom Allah willed to gain knowledge of the religion, so He facilitated that for them, and among them are those whose misguidance and ignorance He willed, so they moved away from it and were not granted success. And Allah is the Granter of success and the Truth.]] and the varieties of His favours, which is the blessing of religion. So he put first, from the blessing of religion, what is at the highest of its ranks and the furthest of its levels:

This is His bestowal of the Qur'an, its sending down and its teaching, because it is the greatest of Allah's revelations in rank, the highest in station, and the most excellent in its effect in the matters of religion. It is the summit (sinam) of the heavenly Books, their confirmation, and the standard by which they are measured. He delayed the mention of the creation of man after mentioning it, and then followed it with it, so that it would be known that He created him only for the religion, and that he might come to know His revelation and His Books, and that for which man was created. It is as if the purpose in his origination was preceding him and prior to him. Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech (al-bayan), which is the articulate language that expresses what is in the heart [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech, which is the clear, articulate language... etc." Ahmad said: He singled out the first sentences for mention only as a rebuke to man, because of the attachment of their meanings to him. Do you not see that he is mentioned in them explicitly, implicitly, and by omission indicated by the context? So he is spoken of openly in His words ﴿He created man﴾, implicitly in His words ﴿He taught him the bayan﴾, and indicated by omission in His words ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, for it is the second object. As for His words ﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate﴾, there is absolutely no mention of man in them, and most of the purpose of their context is to alert to the greatness of Allah, Exalted.]] ﴿The Most Gracious﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and these verbs together with their pronouns are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifa). Their being free of a conjunction is because they come in the pattern of enumeration, as you say: "Zayd made you rich after poverty, honoured you after humiliation, increased you after scarcity, did to you what no one has done to anyone; so what of His kindness do you deny?"

In this there are great benefits for people, among them knowing the years and calculation. ﴿And the star﴾: and the plant that springs up from the earth without a stem, like herbs. ﴿And the tree﴾: that which has a stem. Their prostration is their submission to Allah in what they were created for, and that they do not refuse, likened to the prostration of the accountable humans in their obedience. If you say: how are these two sentences connected to ﴿the Most Gracious﴾? I say: in them the verbal connection is dispensed with in favour of the connection of meaning, since it is known that the reckoning is His reckoning, and the prostration is to Him and not to other than Him. It is as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him." If you say: how did he omit the conjunction in the first sentences, and then bring it after? I say:

They are rebuked by those first sentences coming in the manner of a threat, so that each sentence stands independently in reproaching those who denied the Most Gracious and His blessings, just as a man who denies the favours of the benefactor is rebuked by enumerating them to him, in the example I mentioned. Then the speech returns to its proper course after the rebuke, in joining what must be joined for the sake of harmony and proximity by means of the conjunction. If you say: what harmony is there between these two sentences, that the conjunction was placed between them? I say: the sun and the moon are heavenly, and the star and the tree are earthly, so between the two categories there is harmony by way of opposition, and the heaven and the earth are never mentioned except as a pair; and the running of the sun and moon by reckoning is of the kind of submission to the command of Allah, so it is fitting with the prostration of the star and the tree. It is said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ means He made it a sign and a sign-post (ayah).

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The man (al-insan) is Adam." And from him also: "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

From Mujahid: "The star (al-najm)": the stars of the sky. ﴿And the heaven He raised﴾: He created it raised and elevated, as He made it the source of His rulings, the origin of His decrees, the place of descent of His commands and prohibitions, and the dwelling of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets. Through this He draws attention to the greatness of His majesty, His dominion and His authority. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. In the reading of Abdullah: ﴿and He lowered the balance﴾. By it He meant everything by which things are weighed and their quantities known, of scale, steelyard, measure and gauge. That is, He created it placed and lowered upon the earth, since He attached to it the rulings of His servants, their decisions, and what He made them responsible for in terms of equity and fairness in their taking and giving. ﴿That you not transgress﴾: lest you transgress; or it is that the "an" is explanatory. Abdullah recited: ﴿la tatghaw﴾ without "an", on the intention of "saying". ﴿And establish the weighing with justice﴾: and make your weighing straight with justice. ﴿And do not skimp in the balance﴾: do not diminish it. This is a command to equity and a prohibition of transgression, which is aggression and excess, and of loss, which is short-measure and deficiency.

The word "balance" is repeated to emphasise the charge concerning it, and to strengthen the command to use it and the urging to it. It has been read: "and the heaven" with a nominative (al-raf'), and "do not skimp" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma and a kasra on the sin, and a fatha as well. It is said: "kharisa al-mizan" (he diminished the balance), "yakhsaruhu" and "yakhsiru." As for the fatha, it is based on the original: "do not skimp in the balance," so the preposition is dropped and the verb is connected. ﴿And the earth He laid out﴾: He spread it out, flattened over the water. ﴿For the creatures (lil-anam)﴾: for the creation, which is everything upon the surface of the earth of living creature. It is said from al-Hasan: "mankind and jinn." So it is like a couch for them, on which they move. ﴿Therein fruit﴾: kinds of what is enjoyed as a delicacy. ﴿And palm-trees (al-akmam)﴾: everything that is enclosed (yukammu), i.e., covered, of fibre, palm-frond and spathe [[His words "wa-sa'fa wa-kafarra" — in the Sihah it says "al-kafara without a ta', and it is the container of the spathe," so perhaps the author's expression is "from its fibre, its frond and its spathe", with "kull" annexed to the pronoun of the palm, as will come in "its fruit, its clusters and its trunks", and the copyist mistook it for the feminine ta' and so cut it off above. (ʿ)]], and all of it is beneficial, just as one benefits from what is enclosed of its fruit, its clusters and its trunks. It is said that al-akmam are the containers of dates; the singular is kimm, with a kasra on the kaf. ﴿And the grain-husk (al-'asf)﴾: the leaves of the crop; it is said it is the chaff. ﴿And the sweet-smelling plant (al-rayhan)﴾: the provision, which is the kernel. He meant in it what is enjoyed of fruits, and what unites enjoyment and nourishment, which is the fruit of the palm, and what is fed upon, which is the grain.

It has been read: "wa-l-rayhani" with a kasra. Its meaning is: "and the grain possessing the husk, which is fodder for livestock, and the sweet plant, which is food for people." With a damma, it is read as "wa-dhu al-rayhan," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun is put in its place.

It is said: its meaning is: "and in it is the sweet-smelling plant which is scented." In the codices of the people of Syria it reads: "and the grain possessing the husk and the sweet plant," meaning: "and He created the grain and the sweet plant," or "and He singled out the grain and the sweet plant." It is permissible that it be meant: "and possessor of the sweet plant," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun put in its place. The address in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ is to the two species (al-thaqalan), by the indication of "the creatures" (al-anam) referring to both of them. And His words ﴿We will surely attend to you, O two species﴾ [are addressed to them].

Allah, Mighty and Exalted, enumerates His blessings (ala'ahu), and He wished to begin with the first thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, enumerates His blessings, and He wished to mention first the thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: We modify this statement in his words "that the creation of man had as its purpose", i.e., the intended meaning of it: that he should come to know the Books and the revelation, and we substitute that the purpose of creating him is that he be called to that, not that this occurs from him. This is the general meaning. Then among people, some are those whom Allah willed to gain knowledge of the religion, so He facilitated that for them, and among them are those whose misguidance and ignorance He willed, so they moved away from it and were not granted success. And Allah is the Granter of success and the Truth.]] and the varieties of His favours, which is the blessing of religion. So he put first, from the blessing of religion, what is at the highest of its ranks and the furthest of its levels:

This is His bestowal of the Qur'an, its sending down and its teaching, because it is the greatest of Allah's revelations in rank, the highest in station, and the most excellent in its effect in the matters of religion. It is the summit (sinam) of the heavenly Books, their confirmation, and the standard by which they are measured. He delayed the mention of the creation of man after mentioning it, and then followed it with it, so that it would be known that He created him only for the religion, and that he might come to know His revelation and His Books, and that for which man was created. It is as if the purpose in his origination was preceding him and prior to him. Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech (al-bayan), which is the articulate language that expresses what is in the heart [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech, which is the clear, articulate language... etc." Ahmad said: He singled out the first sentences for mention only as a rebuke to man, because of the attachment of their meanings to him. Do you not see that he is mentioned in them explicitly, implicitly, and by omission indicated by the context? So he is spoken of openly in His words ﴿He created man﴾, implicitly in His words ﴿He taught him the bayan﴾, and indicated by omission in His words ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, for it is the second object. As for His words ﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate﴾, there is absolutely no mention of man in them, and most of the purpose of their context is to alert to the greatness of Allah, Exalted.]] ﴿The Most Gracious﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and these verbs together with their pronouns are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifa). Their being free of a conjunction is because they come in the pattern of enumeration, as you say: "Zayd made you rich after poverty, honoured you after humiliation, increased you after scarcity, did to you what no one has done to anyone; so what of His kindness do you deny?"

In this there are great benefits for people, among them knowing the years and calculation. ﴿And the star﴾: and the plant that springs up from the earth without a stem, like herbs. ﴿And the tree﴾: that which has a stem. Their prostration is their submission to Allah in what they were created for, and that they do not refuse, likened to the prostration of the accountable humans in their obedience. If you say: how are these two sentences connected to ﴿the Most Gracious﴾? I say: in them the verbal connection is dispensed with in favour of the connection of meaning, since it is known that the reckoning is His reckoning, and the prostration is to Him and not to other than Him. It is as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him." If you say: how did he omit the conjunction in the first sentences, and then bring it after? I say:

They are rebuked by those first sentences coming in the manner of a threat, so that each sentence stands independently in reproaching those who denied the Most Gracious and His blessings, just as a man who denies the favours of the benefactor is rebuked by enumerating them to him, in the example I mentioned. Then the speech returns to its proper course after the rebuke, in joining what must be joined for the sake of harmony and proximity by means of the conjunction. If you say: what harmony is there between these two sentences, that the conjunction was placed between them? I say: the sun and the moon are heavenly, and the star and the tree are earthly, so between the two categories there is harmony by way of opposition, and the heaven and the earth are never mentioned except as a pair; and the running of the sun and moon by reckoning is of the kind of submission to the command of Allah, so it is fitting with the prostration of the star and the tree. It is said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ means He made it a sign and a sign-post (ayah).

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The man (al-insan) is Adam." And from him also: "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

From Mujahid: "The star (al-najm)": the stars of the sky. ﴿And the heaven He raised﴾: He created it raised and elevated, as He made it the source of His rulings, the origin of His decrees, the place of descent of His commands and prohibitions, and the dwelling of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets. Through this He draws attention to the greatness of His majesty, His dominion and His authority. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. In the reading of Abdullah: ﴿and He lowered the balance﴾. By it He meant everything by which things are weighed and their quantities known, of scale, steelyard, measure and gauge. That is, He created it placed and lowered upon the earth, since He attached to it the rulings of His servants, their decisions, and what He made them responsible for in terms of equity and fairness in their taking and giving. ﴿That you not transgress﴾: lest you transgress; or it is that the "an" is explanatory. Abdullah recited: ﴿la tatghaw﴾ without "an", on the intention of "saying". ﴿And establish the weighing with justice﴾: and make your weighing straight with justice. ﴿And do not skimp in the balance﴾: do not diminish it. This is a command to equity and a prohibition of transgression, which is aggression and excess, and of loss, which is short-measure and deficiency.

The word "balance" is repeated to emphasise the charge concerning it, and to strengthen the command to use it and the urging to it. It has been read: "and the heaven" with a nominative (al-raf'), and "do not skimp" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma and a kasra on the sin, and a fatha as well. It is said: "kharisa al-mizan" (he diminished the balance), "yakhsaruhu" and "yakhsiru." As for the fatha, it is based on the original: "do not skimp in the balance," so the preposition is dropped and the verb is connected. ﴿And the earth He laid out﴾: He spread it out, flattened over the water. ﴿For the creatures (lil-anam)﴾: for the creation, which is everything upon the surface of the earth of living creature. It is said from al-Hasan: "mankind and jinn." So it is like a couch for them, on which they move. ﴿Therein fruit﴾: kinds of what is enjoyed as a delicacy. ﴿And palm-trees (al-akmam)﴾: everything that is enclosed (yukammu), i.e., covered, of fibre, palm-frond and spathe [[His words "wa-sa'fa wa-kafarra" — in the Sihah it says "al-kafara without a ta', and it is the container of the spathe," so perhaps the author's expression is "from its fibre, its frond and its spathe", with "kull" annexed to the pronoun of the palm, as will come in "its fruit, its clusters and its trunks", and the copyist mistook it for the feminine ta' and so cut it off above. (ʿ)]], and all of it is beneficial, just as one benefits from what is enclosed of its fruit, its clusters and its trunks. It is said that al-akmam are the containers of dates; the singular is kimm, with a kasra on the kaf. ﴿And the grain-husk (al-'asf)﴾: the leaves of the crop; it is said it is the chaff. ﴿And the sweet-smelling plant (al-rayhan)﴾: the provision, which is the kernel. He meant in it what is enjoyed of fruits, and what unites enjoyment and nourishment, which is the fruit of the palm, and what is fed upon, which is the grain.

It has been read: "wa-l-rayhani" with a kasra. Its meaning is: "and the grain possessing the husk, which is fodder for livestock, and the sweet plant, which is food for people." With a damma, it is read as "wa-dhu al-rayhan," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun is put in its place.

It is said: its meaning is: "and in it is the sweet-smelling plant which is scented." In the codices of the people of Syria it reads: "and the grain possessing the husk and the sweet plant," meaning: "and He created the grain and the sweet plant," or "and He singled out the grain and the sweet plant." It is permissible that it be meant: "and possessor of the sweet plant," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun put in its place. The address in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ is to the two species (al-thaqalan), by the indication of "the creatures" (al-anam) referring to both of them. And His words ﴿We will surely attend to you, O two species﴾ [are addressed to them].

Allah, Mighty and Exalted, enumerates His blessings (ala'ahu), and He wished to begin with the first thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, enumerates His blessings, and He wished to mention first the thing that precedes all other kinds of His blessings... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: We modify this statement in his words "that the creation of man had as its purpose", i.e., the intended meaning of it: that he should come to know the Books and the revelation, and we substitute that the purpose of creating him is that he be called to that, not that this occurs from him. This is the general meaning. Then among people, some are those whom Allah willed to gain knowledge of the religion, so He facilitated that for them, and among them are those whose misguidance and ignorance He willed, so they moved away from it and were not granted success. And Allah is the Granter of success and the Truth.]] and the varieties of His favours, which is the blessing of religion. So he put first, from the blessing of religion, what is at the highest of its ranks and the furthest of its levels:

This is His bestowal of the Qur'an, its sending down and its teaching, because it is the greatest of Allah's revelations in rank, the highest in station, and the most excellent in its effect in the matters of religion. It is the summit (sinam) of the heavenly Books, their confirmation, and the standard by which they are measured. He delayed the mention of the creation of man after mentioning it, and then followed it with it, so that it would be known that He created him only for the religion, and that he might come to know His revelation and His Books, and that for which man was created. It is as if the purpose in his origination was preceding him and prior to him. Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech (al-bayan), which is the articulate language that expresses what is in the heart [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "Then He mentioned what distinguished him from the rest of the animals: eloquent speech, which is the clear, articulate language... etc." Ahmad said: He singled out the first sentences for mention only as a rebuke to man, because of the attachment of their meanings to him. Do you not see that he is mentioned in them explicitly, implicitly, and by omission indicated by the context? So he is spoken of openly in His words ﴿He created man﴾, implicitly in His words ﴿He taught him the bayan﴾, and indicated by omission in His words ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾, for it is the second object. As for His words ﴿The sun and the moon are by a reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate﴾, there is absolutely no mention of man in them, and most of the purpose of their context is to alert to the greatness of Allah, Exalted.]] ﴿The Most Gracious﴾ is the subject (mubtada'), and these verbs together with their pronouns are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifa). Their being free of a conjunction is because they come in the pattern of enumeration, as you say: "Zayd made you rich after poverty, honoured you after humiliation, increased you after scarcity, did to you what no one has done to anyone; so what of His kindness do you deny?"

﴿By a reckoning﴾: by a known calculation and a sound measure. ﴿Both run﴾: in their orbits and their stations. In this there are great benefits for people, among them knowing the years and calculation. ﴿And the star﴾: and the plant that springs up from the earth without a stem, like herbs. ﴿And the tree﴾: that which has a stem. Their prostration is their submission to Allah in what they were created for, and that they do not refuse, likened to the prostration of the accountable humans in their obedience. If you say: how are these two sentences connected to ﴿the Most Gracious﴾? I say: in them the verbal connection is dispensed with in favour of the connection of meaning, since it is known that the reckoning is His reckoning, and the prostration is to Him and not to other than Him. It is as if it were said: "The sun and the moon are by His reckoning, and the star and the tree prostrate to Him." If you say: how did he omit the conjunction in the first sentences, and then bring it after? I say:

They are rebuked by those first sentences coming in the manner of a threat, so that each sentence stands independently in reproaching those who denied the Most Gracious and His blessings, just as a man who denies the favours of the benefactor is rebuked by enumerating them to him, in the example I mentioned. Then the speech returns to its proper course after the rebuke, in joining what must be joined for the sake of harmony and proximity by means of the conjunction. If you say: what harmony is there between these two sentences, that the conjunction was placed between them? I say: the sun and the moon are heavenly, and the star and the tree are earthly, so between the two categories there is harmony by way of opposition, and the heaven and the earth are never mentioned except as a pair; and the running of the sun and moon by reckoning is of the kind of submission to the command of Allah, so it is fitting with the prostration of the star and the tree. It is said: ﴿He taught the Qur'an﴾ means He made it a sign and a sign-post (ayah).

From Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The man (al-insan) is Adam." And from him also: "Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

From Mujahid: "The star (al-najm)": the stars of the sky. ﴿And the heaven He raised﴾: He created it raised and elevated, as He made it the source of His rulings, the origin of His decrees, the place of descent of His commands and prohibitions, and the dwelling of His angels who descend with revelation to His prophets. Through this He draws attention to the greatness of His majesty, His dominion and His authority. ﴿And He set up the balance﴾. In the reading of Abdullah: ﴿and He lowered the balance﴾. By it He meant everything by which things are weighed and their quantities known, of scale, steelyard, measure and gauge. That is, He created it placed and lowered upon the earth, since He attached to it the rulings of His servants, their decisions, and what He made them responsible for in terms of equity and fairness in their taking and giving. ﴿That you not transgress﴾: lest you transgress; or it is that the "an" is explanatory. Abdullah recited: ﴿la tatghaw﴾ without "an", on the intention of "saying". ﴿And establish the weighing with justice﴾: and make your weighing straight with justice. ﴿And do not skimp in the balance﴾: do not diminish it. This is a command to equity and a prohibition of transgression, which is aggression and excess, and of loss, which is short-measure and deficiency.

The word "balance" is repeated to emphasise the charge concerning it, and to strengthen the command to use it and the urging to it. It has been read: "and the heaven" with a nominative (al-raf'), and "do not skimp" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma and a kasra on the sin, and a fatha as well. It is said: "kharisa al-mizan" (he diminished the balance), "yakhsaruhu" and "yakhsiru." As for the fatha, it is based on the original: "do not skimp in the balance," so the preposition is dropped and the verb is connected. ﴿And the earth He laid out﴾: He spread it out, flattened over the water. ﴿For the creatures (lil-anam)﴾: for the creation, which is everything upon the surface of the earth of living creature. It is said from al-Hasan: "mankind and jinn." So it is like a couch for them, on which they move. ﴿Therein fruit﴾: kinds of what is enjoyed as a delicacy. ﴿And palm-trees (al-akmam)﴾: everything that is enclosed (yukammu), i.e., covered, of fibre, palm-frond and spathe [[His words "wa-sa'fa wa-kafarra" — in the Sihah it says "al-kafara without a ta', and it is the container of the spathe," so perhaps the author's expression is "from its fibre, its frond and its spathe", with "kull" annexed to the pronoun of the palm, as will come in "its fruit, its clusters and its trunks", and the copyist mistook it for the feminine ta' and so cut it off above. (ʿ)]], and all of it is beneficial, just as one benefits from what is enclosed of its fruit, its clusters and its trunks. It is said that al-akmam are the containers of dates; the singular is kimm, with a kasra on the kaf. ﴿And the grain-husk (al-'asf)﴾: the leaves of the crop; it is said it is the chaff. ﴿And the sweet-smelling plant (al-rayhan)﴾: the provision, which is the kernel. He meant in it what is enjoyed of fruits, and what unites enjoyment and nourishment, which is the fruit of the palm, and what is fed upon, which is the grain.

It has been read: "wa-l-rayhani" with a kasra. Its meaning is: "and the grain possessing the husk, which is fodder for livestock, and the sweet plant, which is food for people." With a damma, it is read as "wa-dhu al-rayhan," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun is put in its place.

It is said: its meaning is: "and in it is the sweet-smelling plant which is scented." In the codices of the people of Syria it reads: "and the grain possessing the husk and the sweet plant," meaning: "and He created the grain and the sweet plant," or "and He singled out the grain and the sweet plant." It is permissible that it be meant: "and possessor of the sweet plant," so the annexed noun is omitted and the annexed-to noun put in its place. The address in ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ is to the two species (al-thaqalan), by the indication of "the creatures" (al-anam) referring to both of them. And His words ﴿We will surely attend to you, O two species﴾ [are addressed to them].

Al-ṣalṣāl: dried clay that has a ringing sound (ṣalṣala). Al-fakhkhār: clay that has been fired by fire, i.e. pottery (al-khazaf).

If you say: the revelation has varied on this, as in His words, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿from black mud, moulded﴾ and ﴿from sticky clay﴾, and "from dust". I say: it is agreed in meaning, and it indicates that He created him from dust: He made it clay, then black mud moulded, then ṣalṣāl.

Al-jānn is the father of the jinn. It is said: he is Iblis. And al-mārij: the pure flame that has no smoke in it. It is said: that which is mixed with the blackness of fire, from "maraja al-shay'" when it is agitated and mixed.

If you say: what is the meaning of His words ﴿from fire﴾? I say: it is an explanation of al-mārij, as if it were said: from pure fire.

Or: mixed from fire; or He intended a specific fire, like His words, Exalted is He, ﴿So I have warned you of a Fire that blazes﴾.

**Surah 55, verses 19–23 — Al-Zamakhshari, al-Kashshaf**

﴿مَرَجَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ﴾ — He let loose the two seas: He sent forth the salt sea and the sweet sea, adjacent and meeting, with no separation visible to the eye between the two waters.

﴿بَيْنَهُمَا بَرْزَخٌ﴾ — between them is a barrier (barzakh, a partition or isthmus): a barrier from the power of God, the Exalted.

﴿لَا يَبْغِيَانِ﴾ — they do not transgress: they do not exceed their limits, and neither of them oversteps against the other by mixing.

It is read ﴿يخرج﴾ and ﴿يخرج﴾ (with the verb in the form meaning "it comes out" / "it is brought out" with ﴿مَنْ أَخْرَجَ﴾ as a variant), and ﴿وخرج﴾ and ﴿يَخْرُجُ﴾, meaning: God, the Mighty and Majestic, brings forth ﴿اللُّؤْلُؤُ وَالْمَرْجَانُ﴾ (the pearl and the coral), with the accusative case, and ﴿نُخْرِجُ﴾ with the letter nun.

﴿اللُّؤْلُؤُ﴾ (lu'lu'): pearls. ﴿الْمَرْجَانُ﴾ (marjan): this red bead, which is the bead (bazd). It has been said: ﴿اللُّؤْلُؤُ﴾ is the large pearls, and ﴿الْمَرْجَانُ﴾ is their small ones.

If you say: why did He say ﴿مِنْهُمَا﴾ ("from both of them") when they come out only from the salt water? [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, why did He say 'from both of them' when they come out only from the salt water... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This second answer is refuted by observation, and the correct one is the first. Similar is the verse ﴿لَوْلَا نُزِّلَ هَذَا الْقُرْآنُ عَلَى رَجُلٍ مِنَ الْقَرْيَتَيْنِ عَظِيمٍ﴾ ("Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from the two towns?"), where only one of the two towns is intended. This is the correct and evident view, just as you say: "So-and-so is from the people of the cities of Egypt," when his city is only one quarter of them.]]? I say: when the two met and became like one thing, it was permissible to say "they come out from them," just as one says "they come out from the sea," though they do not come out from the whole sea but from part of it.

And you say: "I went out from the town," though I went out only from a quarter of its quarters, indeed from a single house of its houses.

It has also been said: they come out only from the meeting place of the salt and the sweet.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 55, verses 31–32:

"Sanafrughu lakum" is borrowed from the saying of a man to one who threatens him: "Sa-afrughu laka" (I will be free for you), meaning: I will devote myself to bringing you down, free from everything that occupies me away from you, so that I have no occupation other than that. The intended meaning is to devote oneself to harming him and taking revenge on him. It is also permissible to understand it as: the world will come to an end and reach its last, and with that the affairs of creation that He referred to in His saying ﴿every day He is in an affair﴾ will come to an end, so nothing remains but one affair, which is your recompense. Thus He made that "freedom" for them by way of a figure of speech (mathal).

It was also read as "Sayafrughu lakum", meaning: God Most High will be free for you; and "Sa-afrughu lakum" (with the first person); and "Sanafrughu" with the nun, vowelled with a fatha and with a kasra, and with a fatha on the ra'; and "Sayafrughu" with the ya', vowelled with a fatha and with a damma, along with a fatha on the ra'. In the reading of Ubayy it is "Sanafrughu ilaykum", meaning: We will turn towards you (sanaqsidu ilaykum).

"Al-thaqalan" (the two weighty ones) are mankind and the jinn; they were so named because they are the two burdens of the earth.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 55, verses 33–36:

﴿O assembly of jinn and humankind﴾ is an explanation of His words, "O you two weighty ones" (al-thaqalan). ﴿If you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass beyond them. You will not pass except with authority﴾ means: if you are able to escape My decree and leave My dominion, My heaven and My earth, then do so. Then He said: ﴿You will not pass except with authority﴾, meaning with strength, compulsion and force, ﴿and how could you have that?﴾, and similar to it: ﴿and you cannot escape in the earth or in the heaven﴾.

It is narrated that the angels, peace be upon them, will descend and surround all creation. When the jinn and humankind see them, they will flee, but they will find that the angels have encircled wherever they turn.

It was recited as "shuwazun" (flame) and "nuhasun" (smoke), both with a ḍamma and with a kasra. The shuwaz is pure flame. The nuhas is smoke, and he recited:

It shines like the light of the lamp of sesame oil, ... God has not placed in it any smoke (nuhas).

Here "lam yaj'al" (has not placed) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to "the lamp" (al-sirāj). The condition for a ḥāl to come from the mudāf ilayh (the second term of an idafa) is present, since the light is like its part. Perhaps he is describing the face of his beloved, about whom he said:

When her bedfellow bends her side... the verse.

He likened it to a lamp in its brightness, on the condition that there is no smoke in it, because the light of her face is likewise. So this is a restricted (muqayyad) simile.

It has also been said: molten brass (al-ṣufr al-muḏāb) is poured over their heads. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, that when they come out of their graves, a flame (shuwaz) drives them to the place of gathering.

It was also recited as "wa-nuhāsun" in the nominative, coordinated with "shuwaz", and in the genitive, coordinated with "nār" (fire). It was recited as "wa-nuḥsun", the plural of nuhās, like liḥāf and liḥf. It was also recited as "wa-nuḥsu", meaning: and we will be destroyed by the punishment.

It was recited: ﴿We will send upon you both a flame of fire and smoke, and you will not be able to defend yourselves﴾, meaning: you will not be able to resist.

خَيْراتٌ خيرات فخففت، كقوله عليه السلام «هينون لينون» [[قوله «هينون لينون» لعله ورد في صفة المؤمنين ومثله قال الشاعر:

هينون لينون أيسار ذوو كرم (ع)]] وأما «خير» الذي هو بمعنى أخير، فلا يقال فيه خيرون ولا خيرات. وقرئ: خيرات على الأصل. والمعنى:

Khayrat khayrat (خَيْراتٌ خيرات) was lightened (fakhuffifat), as in the Prophet's saying, peace be upon him: "Hayyinun layyinun" (هينون لينون) [[The saying "hayyinun layyinun" may have been transmitted in description of the believers, and the poet said similarly:

Gentle and soft, generous and noble of lineage (ع)]]. As for "khayr" (خير) in the sense of "akhayr" (أخير, more excellent), one does not say "khayrun" or "khayrat" of it. It was also read "khayrat" in its original form. The meaning is:

Virtuous in character, good in disposition (فاضلات الأخلاق حسان الخلق). "Maqsurat" (مَقْصُوراتٌ): they are confined, confined in their tents (قصرن في خدورهنّ). It is said: "imra'a qasira," "qasura," and "maqsura mukhaddara" (a woman who is secluded). It is said that a tent among their tents is a hollow pearl. "Qablahum" (قَبْلَهُمْ): before them, i.e., before the people of the two gardens, whose mention of the two gardens indicates them. "Muttaki'in" (مُتَّكِئِينَ) is in the accusative as a specification (نصب على الاختصاص, a grammatical construction in which a noun is singled out for mention). "Rafraf" (الرفرف) is a kind of carpet. It is said: carpets; it is said: cushions; it is said: every wide garment is a rafraf. The edges of carpets and the excess of tent-cloth are called "rafarif." "Rafraf al-sahab" (ورفرف السحاب) is its hedab (هيدبه, the fringe, lowest hanging part of clouds) [[The saying "warafraf al-sahab hayduhu" (ورفرف السحاب هيديه): in al-Sihah (الصحاح): "haydab al-sahab" is what hangs down from it; when one wants the foliage, one means it as if they were threads. (ع)]]. "Al-'abqari" (العبقري) is attributed to "Abqar," which the Arabs claim is the land of the jinn, so they attribute to it every marvelous thing. It was also read "rafarif khudr" with two dammas. "'Abaqari," like "madaʼini," is a nisba (relative adjective) to "'Abaqari" as a place name. Abu Hatim transmitted "'abaqara" with fatha on the qaf and without tanwin, but this has no valid basis. If you ask: how were the attributes of these two gardens reduced compared with the first two, so that it was said: "wa-min dunihima" (﴿وَمِن دُونِهِمَا﴾, "and beneath them")?

I say: "mudhammatan" (مدهامّتان) is lower than "dhawata afnan" (ذواتا أفنان). "Nadikhatan" (ونضاختان) is lower than "tajriyan" (تجريان). "Fakiha" (وفاكهة) is lower than "kullu fakiha" (كل فاكهة, every fruit).

And likewise the description of the maidens (al-hur) and the reclining couches (al-mutaka'). It was also read "dhu al-jalal" (ذو الجلال) as an attribute of the Name.

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surah al-Rahman has rendered the thanks for what Allah has bestowed upon him." [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, al-Wahidi and Ibn Mardawayh with their chains going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]]
